time-dependent-generalized-coordinate-c0.title: Time-Dependent Generalized Coordinate
time-dependent-generalized-coordinate-c0.description: This expression represents the i-th generalized coordinate of a physical system as a function of time, describing its evolution.
time-dependent-generalized-coordinate-c0.conceptual_definition: In analytical mechanics, generalized coordinates, denoted by $q_i$, are a minimal set of independent variables that completely specify the configuration of a system at any given time. The notation $q_i(t)$ explicitly indicates that these coordinates are functions of time, meaning their values change as the system evolves. This time dependence is what the Euler-Lagrange equations ultimately aim to determine.
time-dependent-generalized-coordinate-c0.interpretation: The function $q_i(t)$ provides the complete kinematic description of the i-th degree of freedom of a system. When all $q_i(t)$ for a system are known, the exact position and orientation of every particle in the system can be determined at any instant. The specific form of $q_i(t)$ for a given system is found by solving the Euler-Lagrange differential equations, which are derived from the system's Lagrangian. Thus, $q_i(t)$ represents the actual physical trajectory or motion of the system in its configuration space.
time-dependent-generalized-coordinate-c0.limits_and_boundary: The domain and range of $q_i(t)$ are specific to the physical system and the chosen coordinate system. For instance, if $q_i$ is an angle, its range might be $[0, 2\pi)$, while if it's a linear position, it could be $(-\infty, \infty)$. The specific solution for $q_i(t)$ is uniquely determined by initial conditions, typically $q_i(t_0)$ and $\dot{q}_i(t_0)$, which specify the system's initial configuration and velocity.
time-dependent-generalized-coordinate-c0.symmetry_origin: The choice of generalized coordinates can often be made to exploit the symmetries of a system, simplifying the Lagrangian. If the Lagrangian $L$ does not explicitly depend on a particular generalized coordinate $q_i$ (i.e., $q_i$ is cyclic), then the canonical momentum conjugate to $q_i$, $p_i = \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot{q}_i}$, is a conserved quantity. This conservation law is a direct consequence of Noether's theorem, linking symmetry to conservation.

product-of-squared-state-norms-fb4a8a01.title: Product of Squared State Norms
product-of-squared-state-norms-fb4a8a01.description: The product of the squared Hilbert space norms of two quantum state vectors, forming the upper bound in the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.
product-of-squared-state-norms-fb4a8a01.conceptual_definition: In the mathematical framework of quantum mechanics and Hilbert spaces $\mathcal{H}$, the product of squared state norms $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle \langle\phi|\phi\rangle = \|\psi\|^2 \|\phi\|^2$ represents the scalar product of the self-inner products of two vectors $|\psi\rangle, |\phi\rangle \in \mathcal{H}$. By positive-definiteness of the inner product, this quantity is strictly non-negative and vanishes if and only if at least one of the state vectors is the zero vector.
product-of-squared-state-norms-fb4a8a01.interpretation: The term $\langle\psi|\psi\rangle$ denotes the inner product of the state vector $|\psi\rangle$ with its dual bra vector $\langle\psi|$, representing the square of the $L^2$-norm $\|\psi\|^2$. Similarly, $\langle\phi|\phi\rangle$ represents $\|\phi\|^2$ for state vector $|\phi\rangle$. When both states are physically normalized pure states, each norm equals $1$, rendering the product equal to unity. In the general unnormalized setting, it establishes the standard right-hand side of the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality $|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^2 \le \langle\phi|\phi\rangle \langle\psi|\psi\rangle$.
product-of-squared-state-norms-fb4a8a01.limits_and_boundary: In the normalized quantum state limit $\|\psi\| \to 1$ and $\|\phi\| \to 1$, the product approaches $1$. If either state approaches the null vector $|0\rangle$, the product continuously vanishes to $0$.
product-of-squared-state-norms-fb4a8a01.symmetry_origin: Unitary invariance ($U(\mathcal{H})$): inner products and norms in Hilbert space are invariant under global unitary transformations $|\psi\rangle \mapsto \hat{U}|\psi\rangle$ and $|\phi\rangle \mapsto \hat{U}|\phi\rangle$, preserving the product of squared norms.

kinetic-energy-relative-to-center-of-mas.title: Kinetic Energy Relative to Center of Mass
kinetic-energy-relative-to-center-of-mas.description: This equation represents the total kinetic energy of a system of particles as observed from a reference frame moving with the system's center of mass. It quantifies the internal motion of the system.
kinetic-energy-relative-to-center-of-mas.conceptual_definition: The kinetic energy of a system of particles as measured in a reference frame co-moving with the system's center of mass. It represents the energy of the system's internal motion, such as rotation and vibration, independent of its overall translational motion.
kinetic-energy-relative-to-center-of-mas.interpretation: König's theorem decomposes the total kinetic energy of a system into two parts: the kinetic energy of the center of mass, $\frac{1}{2} M |\mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{cm}}|^2$, and the kinetic energy relative to the center of mass, $K_{\mathrm{rel}}$. The term $K_{\mathrm{rel}} = \sum_{i} \frac{1}{2} m_i |\mathbf{v}_{i, \mathrm{rel}}|^2$ isolates the energy associated with the system's internal dynamics, where $\mathbf{v}_{i, \mathrm{rel}} = \mathbf{v}_i - \mathbf{V}_{\mathrm{cm}}$. For a rigid body, this internal energy is purely rotational, simplifying to $K_{\mathrm{rel}} = \frac{1}{2} I_{\mathrm{cm}} \omega^2$, where $I_{\mathrm{cm}}$ is the moment of inertia about the center of mass and $\omega$ is the angular velocity.
kinetic-energy-relative-to-center-of-mas.limits_and_boundary:
1. Rigid Body Limit: For a rigid body rotating with angular velocity $\omega$ about its center of mass, the relative kinetic energy becomes the rotational kinetic energy: $K_{\mathrm{rel}} = \frac{1}{2} I_{\mathrm{cm}} \omega^2$.
2. Static Internal State: If all particles are at rest relative to the center of mass (e.g., a non-rotating, non-vibrating object), then all $\mathbf{v}_{i, \mathrm{rel}} = 0$ and $K_{\mathrm{rel}} = 0$.
3. Two-Body System: For a two-body system with masses $m_1$ and $m_2$, the relative kinetic energy is $K_{\mathrm{rel}} = \frac{1}{2} \mu |\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{rel}}|^2$, where $\mu = \frac{m_1 m_2}{m_1 + m_2}$ is the reduced mass and $\mathbf{v}_{\mathrm{rel}} = \mathbf{v}_1 - \mathbf{v}_2$ is the relative velocity between the two particles.
kinetic-energy-relative-to-center-of-mas.symmetry_origin: The decomposition of kinetic energy into center-of-mass and relative components is a direct consequence of Galilean relativity, where velocities add linearly. The internal kinetic energy term is invariant under boosts of the laboratory frame. For an isolated system, the total energy, including this internal kinetic energy, is conserved due to time-translation symmetry (Noether's theorem).

timelike-spacetime-interval-condition-5d.title: Timelike Spacetime Interval Condition
timelike-spacetime-interval-condition-5d.description: Defines the geometric criterion for a timelike separation between two events in Minkowski spacetime under the mostly-minus $(+,-,-,-)$ metric signature.
timelike-spacetime-interval-condition-5d.conceptual_definition: A spacetime interval is classified as timelike when the invariant squared interval satisfies $ds^2 = c^2 dt^2 - d\mathbf{x}^2 > 0$ (or equivalently $\eta_{\mu\nu} dx^\mu dx^\nu > 0$). For timelike separated events, a physical observer or causal massive signal traveling at subluminal speed $v < c$ can traverse between them, and there exists a Lorentz frame in which both events occur at the exact same spatial location.
timelike-spacetime-interval-condition-5d.interpretation: In the timelike condition $ds^2 > 0$, the temporal separation dominates the spatial separation such that $c^2 dt^2 > d\mathbf{x}^2$. The real proper time elapsed along the worldline connecting the two events is given by $d\tau = \sqrt{ds^2}/c = dt \sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$, representing the physical clock time experienced by a co-moving observer.
timelike-spacetime-interval-condition-5d.limits_and_boundary: As the spatial velocity $v \to c$, the interval approaches the null boundary $ds^2 \to 0$ (lightlike separation). For $v > c$, the interval transitions to the spacelike domain $ds^2 < 0$, precluding causal contact.
timelike-spacetime-interval-condition-5d.symmetry_origin: Lorentz invariance $SO(1,3)$ and Poincaré symmetry, which preserve the Minkowski metric tensor $\eta_{\mu\nu}$ and the sign of the spacetime interval under all proper orthochronous Lorentz boosts and rotations.

normal-derivative-operator-1fff8b99.description: A differential operator representing the directional derivative along the unit normal vector to a surface, commonly applied in boundary value problems and flux definitions.

position-momentum-commutation-relation-1.title: Position-Momentum Canonical Commutation Relation
position-momentum-commutation-relation-1.description: Fundamental quantum relation establishing the non-commutativity of the position and momentum operators, forming the operator-theoretic foundation for the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle.
position-momentum-commutation-relation-1.conceptual_definition: The position-momentum commutation relation $[\hat{x}, \hat{p}] = i\hbar$ establishes that the coordinate operator $\hat{x}$ and its canonically conjugate momentum operator $\hat{p}$ do not commute on the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H} = L^2(\mathbb{R})$. As a consequence of Dirac's canonical quantization rule $[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] = i\hbar \{A, B\}_{\text{PB}}$, this non-vanishing commutator replaces the classical Poisson bracket $\{x, p\} = 1$, precluding the existence of a joint basis of eigenstates for position and momentum.
position-momentum-commutation-relation-1.interpretation: The commutator $[\hat{x}, \hat{p}] = \hat{x}\hat{p} - \hat{p}\hat{x}$ evaluates to the constant operator $i\hbar \hat{\mathbb{I}}$. The presence of the imaginary unit $i$ ensures the self-adjointness of physical observables, while the reduced Planck constant $\hbar$ sets the characteristic quantum scale of action. Because the commutator is non-zero ($i\hbar \neq 0$), the Robertson-Schrödinger relation immediately mandates the lower bound on product variances $\sigma_x \sigma_p \ge \hbar/2$.
position-momentum-commutation-relation-1.limits_and_boundary: Classical limit ($\hbar \to 0$): $[\hat{x}, \hat{p}] \to 0$, recovering the classical phase space where position $x$ and momentum $p$ are freely commuting $c$-number coordinates.
position-momentum-commutation-relation-1.symmetry_origin: Spatial translation symmetry and the Stone-von Neumann theorem: the momentum operator $\hat{p} = -i\hbar \frac{\partial}{\partial x}$ acts as the infinitesimal generator of spatial translations corresponding to the Lie algebra of the Heisenberg group $\mathbb{H}_3$.
